rv.q: Most of all, An Oak Tree remains a beautiful landmark of experimental theatre.
Tim Crouch puts another batch of guest stars through the emotional wringer of this theatrical experiment in empathy and vulnerability
If you get lucky, you are in for an absolute treat.
As with the Michael Craig-Martin artwork it references, I can admire the concept and the artistry of the piece, while not entirely connecting to it on an emotional level.
I urge you to go and experience this for yourselves.

Tim Crouch's theatrical experiment still holds weight, and that even the sceptics among us (me) can appreciate the way form and structure are played with, twisted, and occasionally abandoned altogether.
An unusual, funny, and surprisingly moving production that's well worth experiencing.
Yet while I respected An Oak Tree, I rarely felt emotionally invested in it.
The more fascinating the theatrical experiment becomes, the harder it is to engage with the human story at its centre.

cn.t: Crouch's experimental two-hander, featuring a different unprepared guest actor each night, remains a compelling meditation on grief and theatrical illusion two decades on, though its conceptual audacity impresses more than it emotionally devastates.
